INTRODUCTIONEXECUTIVE SUMMARY

Ground the future in reality.

The proof is the work you can see, touch and feel. TerraFirma is bridging the present to the future, and we are spreading this mission across the country, the world and the galaxy.

THE CAMPAIGN

An activation and recruiting experience in ten cities. Pop-up Playgrounds let anyone run a real TerraFirma demo and mission control center.

THE GOAL

Fill TerraFirma’s open roles in engineering, operations and construction, and make it a name every builder knows, across the physical and digital world.

THE STYLE

Daylight billboards in the colors of the HQ mural, with one neon-orange word on each. Every billboard reads left to right: the Operator in local gear, the city’s skyline, a TerraFirma excavator at work, and rockets rising in front of Mars.

10cities8 wkslive3budget tiers, from ~$428K to ~$3.1M

LEADERSHIP ASKSDECISIONS BEFORE LAUNCH

What we need from leadership.

Three decisions get this campaign from concept to a plan we can price and run.

Pick the launch scope.

Decide whether to prove the idea in four cities with Pilot or take the same budget per city to all ten with Core. Approve a spending ceiling before we ask vendors to hold space.

Approve the creative and rights.

Choose the strongest billboard concept and flag any headline you would cut. Connect us with the HQ mural artist to license the Operator, share the official wordmark and approve any local artist outreach.

Confirm the recruiting priorities.

Ask the People team to name the priority roles, clarify which hires need to move to Texas and confirm the careers URL and how we’ll track applications by city.

11 / ACTIVATION & GAMIFICATIONTHE BILLBOARD MAKES THE CLAIM. THE PLAYGROUND PROVES IT.

Don't read the billboard. Drive the machine.

Nobody sits in the machine. That's the point.

Every city gets a pop-up where people run a real TerraFirma machine from a remote station, race through three challenges and post a score to a public leaderboard. Recruiters are waiting at the finish line. And nobody ever stands in line: every visitor books a time or joins a virtual queue on their phone, and gets a text when it’s their turn. That frees them to explore the other displays, exhibits and activations around the Playground while they wait.

The full activation plan
How it works

Every city gets a pop-up TerraFirma Playground: a fenced dirt lot with three real retrofitted machines and a Mission Control container beside it. Visitors don't climb into a cab. They sit at the same remote stations TerraFirma operators use and run a mini excavator, skid steer or track loader from outside the pit. That's the product demo, the safety story and the recruiting pitch at once.

Heavy-equipment playgrounds already sell out as attractions (Dig This in Las Vegas, Extreme Sandbox in Minnesota and Dallas). In theirs you ride in the cab. In ours, you run the machine from a screen, which is exactly the job TerraFirma is hiring for.

FORMAT A

The Playground

An outdoor lot, open to the public for 3–4 days, with three machines, four remote stations, a leaderboard and recruiters on site. It works best in cities with open space and big crowds: Austin, Nashville, LA, Chicago, Miami, NYC and Atlanta.

~$105K–$145K per pop-up, plus a one-time ~$37K container build

FORMAT B

Mission Control Pod

An indoor booth at a conference or in a storefront. Two stations connect live to a real machine at the Texas yard, with a camera feed of the site. It works best where open lots are hard to find or the crowd is indoors: SF, Boston and DC.

~$38K per event, booth included

The game, step by step
1 · Book or join the queueBook a time on the careers page, under your city, before you come, or scan the QR code at the gate to join the virtual queue. Sign the waiver on your phone. Operators must be 18+; younger visitors watch from the rail.
2 · Get the text, then the safety briefYour phone buzzes when you’re 15 minutes out and again when you’re up, so there’s no standing around. Then two minutes with a TerraFirma operator: controls, the e-stop and the rules.
3 · Take the controlsA three-minute run: dig a trench, stack tires or level the “Mars landing pad.”
4 · Get your scoreTime and accuracy go on the leaderboard. That score is your proof of work: earned in a real machine, not claimed on a résumé. Everyone leaves with an "Operator license" card as the receipt.
5 · Meet the teamRecruiters, engineers and real operators on site. Apply on the spot; top scorers get a fast-track interview.
No lines, ever

Nobody stands in a line at a Playground or a Pod. A line wastes the visitor’s time and makes the brand look disorganized, which is the opposite of what a robotics company should show. Instead, every visit runs on a reservation and virtual-queue system, the same way a busy restaurant or theme park handles a wait.

There are two ways in. People who plan ahead book a time slot on the careers page, which the billboards and social posts point to. People who walk up scan a QR code at the gate and join the virtual queue. Either way, they sign the waiver on their phone, get a text when they’re 15 minutes out and another when they’re up, and are free to watch from the rail, visit the recruiter lounge or grab food nearby in the meantime. A screen at the gate shows the current wait, and a host helps anyone without a phone join the queue.

The math keeps the wait honest. Three machines with a short brief and a three-minute run can handle about 40 people an hour, or roughly 350 a day. Slots are released in 15-minute blocks of about ten people, with a few held back for walk-ups and no-shows. Anyone who misses their slot can rebook once.

The queue doubles as a recruiting tool. Every booking captures a name and phone number, so recruiters know who is coming and can follow up with everyone who ran the machine.

What it takes to run one
Machines
Truck TerraFirma's own fleet from Texas, or rent compact machines locally (United Rentals, Sunbelt Rentals) and fit the retrofit kit on site. A dealer partner is worth asking for; Komatsu already supplies Extreme Sandbox.
Site
A private lot with a short-term lease, a temporary-use or special-event permit from the city, dirt delivery and grading, fencing, power and restrooms (United Site Services or a local vendor).
Connectivity
At a Playground, the stations sit right next to the pit on a wired or private network, so there’s almost no delay between moving a control and the machine responding. Pods connect to Texas over fiber, with a backup line. Test that delay before the doors open.
Safety
Nobody goes inside the fence while machines run. There’s a 25-foot buffer, speed limits, and a software “geofence” that stops a machine at the edge of the pit. Every station has an emergency stop, and the TerraFirma safety lead has a master stop for everything.
Queue
A reservation and virtual-queue tool such as Waitwhile handles bookings and walk-ups and sends the text alerts. The web team links it to the waiver and the leaderboard so a booked visitor never has to stop at a desk.
Insurance
The event needs general liability insurance, equipment coverage and signed waivers from participants. Bring in an insurance broker early.
Production
Hire a local event agency to build and staff the site, outfit the Mission Control container and run the LED leaderboard. Add a photo and video crew so every pop-up produces content for social media and for this book.

APPENDIX A / THE SPIKY POINT OF VIEWWHAT WE'RE WILLING TO ARGUE

Mars won't be built by people who've never moved dirt.

TerraFirma is the in-between: the ground we stand on today, and the ground we'll stand on next.

The full argument
Why start with dirt

Most marketing about the future skips straight from today to science fiction, with renderings, demo days and launch videos. TerraFirma’s founders came from SpaceX and chose to start with excavators instead. That choice is the campaign. The road to the Moon and Mars runs through ordinary jobs like a substation in New Braunfels, the groundwork for a Starbucks in North Austin and an arena in Spicewood.

So every billboard does three things. It points to something real and local, it puts TerraFirma’s Operator in front of it, and it leaves rockets on the horizon in the background. The future stays in the picture, but the work comes first.

Proof of work

Proof of work is an idea from Bitcoin. A new block only counts if someone has done real, measurable work to make it, so the effort can’t be faked and anyone can check it. This campaign holds itself to the same standard. Talk is cheap, and moved dirt isn’t.

In practice, that means four things. The billboards point to real job sites instead of renderings. The Playgrounds let people do the work themselves instead of watching a video about it. Every score on the leaderboard is earned in a real machine, and the Operator license card is the receipt. And the fastest way into an interview is a good run, because three minutes at the controls says more than a résumé.

It also fits the people TerraFirma wants to hire. Operators and engineers are judged by what they’ve built, not by what they say they can build. A campaign that leads with proof speaks their language.

What we're against, and what we're for

WE'RE AGAINST

Vapor futurism

  • Renderings sold as progress
  • Careers where nothing you make exists
  • "America can't build anymore"
  • Claims nobody can check

WE'RE FOR

Grounded optimism

  • Machines on real job sites, this week
  • Code that moves 40 tons of earth
  • Hard work that's approachable
  • Proof of work over promises

The OperatorThe chrome-helmeted robot is the campaign's face. The cowboy hat stays in Austin. Every other city dresses him in local gear, and then a local artist does an edition in their own style.
Mars horizonThe future is always in the background, never the foreground. Chrome rockets stand on the horizon of every billboard, drawn like the ones in the mural.

APPENDIX D / GO-TO-MARKET6 WEEKS PREP · 8 WEEKS LIVE

Signal, then ground, then proof.

After six weeks of prep, the campaign runs for eight weeks in three steps. Teaser billboards get people curious, all ten cities launch together, and the pop-up activations prove the claims on the billboards. The final step is proof of work: real photos, real runs and real hires replace every claim in this book. The slowest pieces, the painted walls and artist editions, go up during the first weeks live instead of holding up the launch.

The full rollout
Phase by phase

The stunt

THE STUNT

Operate an excavator in Texas from Times Square.

TerraFirma already runs its machines from a remote control center, so we take a control station on tour. A candidate in Times Square, Wynwood or Kendall Square sits down and moves real dirt on a real Texas site, with a TerraFirma operator beside them. The billboard makes the claim; the booth proves it in under five minutes. It's the most grounded futurism we can show, and it's built for press, short video and on-the-spot interviews.

The Activation & gamification section (page 11) turns this stunt into a full program in every city.

How we'll measure it
Qualified applicantscounted by city, using a “how did you hear about us” question on the application and source tags in the hiring system
Cost per hirecompared with what a recruiting agency would charge for the same roles
Earned mediapress coverage and how often people share photos of the billboards
Booth conversionhow many demo runs turn into interviews

The table shows the three detailed estimates. The Core baseline is $1,070,198.50, calculated by applying the Pilot average of $107,019.85 to ten cities. It includes the Pilot rate’s share of contingency and other shared costs. The final ten-city budget will depend on local quotes.

How the numbers were built

The budget follows the same proof-of-work idea: every number shows its math and links to where it came from. Each line multiplies a quantity by a unit cost, and every unit cost cites a public source on the sheet's Sources tab. Billboard prices come from rate guides by Dash Two and Alluvit Media, the SF skyway prices from the SF Standard, Times Square from AdQuick, and painted walls from Colossal Media's published minimum. Each Playground is built piece by piece in its own block: the lot, permits, dirt, fencing, machines, power, lighting, restrooms, LED screens, staff, security, EMTs, insurance and crew travel. Travel assumes $600 a flight and about $250 a hotel night, plus the federal per diem for meals. Where a source gives a range, the sheet uses the midpoint.

Some costs have no public benchmark, such as lot leases, licensing the Operator and the event agency fee. Those lines are marked as assumptions so they get a vendor quote first. Two numbers are the least certain. No public rates exist for station takeovers in Chicago or DC, so the sheet budgets half of New York's published rate until Intersection (CTA) and Outfront (WMATA) quote them. Insurance for a public machine demo needs a broker quote, so that line is a placeholder.

The budget leaves out referral bonuses, which come from the recruiting budget, TerraFirma staff salaries (including the campaign lead, who runs the project in-house), and the machines and retrofit kits TerraFirma already owns. The average per city divides each tier’s total by its number of cities, so shared costs such as creative, the Mission Control container, digital and contingency are spread evenly.

APPENDIX G / OPEN QUESTIONSANSWER IN THE COMMENTS

What I need from you.

What would the industry argue with?

What is the boldest belief TerraFirma holds about construction? I assumed it was “the operator shouldn’t have to sit in the cab.” Is there something sharper?

Can we run public demos?

Is it realistic to let the public run real machines remotely, given safety, connection delays and insurance? If not, the fallback is a simulator with live video from a real site.

Assumptions in this draft
  • The campaign keeps one master line, but what it argues against changes by city: tech hype in SF, LA and Atlanta, and the “America can’t build anymore” mood in Boston.
  • Local artists are commissioned for real. The Austin Operator is cropped from your HQ mural; the other nine are AI concept art made from it, as placeholders for the artist editions.
  • Texas is the signature on every billboard ("Texas Born, Mars Bound."), including Miami, where only the headline is in Spanish. The cowboy hat belongs to Austin only. Every billboard uses the same bone, ink and neon-orange palette.
  • The city scenes are illustrated mockups, not photographs. Each one can be swapped for a real photo once its billboard goes up.
APPENDIX H / IN THE REAL WORLDAUSTIN, ON A REAL BILLBOARD

What a driver would actually see.

The city pages show each billboard in an illustrated scene. This page puts the Austin design on a real billboard photographed in Austin, with the light arm and catwalk still in front of it, so you can judge it the way someone stuck in traffic would.

How this render was made
Before and after

The left image is the original photo, which shows an older public-health ad. The right image is the same photo with the TerraFirma billboard fitted to the panel. The design was bent to match the billboard's angle and toned down slightly to look like printed vinyl in cloudy daylight. The light arm, the support rod and the catwalk grating were kept from the original photo so they sit in front of the design, exactly as they would in real life.

What changed to fit this billboard

This is a poster billboard, which is shorter and squarer than the long 14-by-48-foot highway billboards the plan buys. Its face is about two and a quarter times as wide as it is tall, while the main design is about three and a half times as wide. Rather than stretch anything, the layout is rebuilt for the taller shape. The headline is about a third larger and fills the top of the billboard, and the skyline, excavator and rockets sit lower so the scene fills the height.

The catwalk and light arm hide roughly the bottom quarter of this billboard. If the design had been placed as-is, the logo and the careers address would have ended up behind the steel. So the headline, the wordmark, the sign-off and the careers address all sit in the top two-thirds, and only the grid floor and the bottom of the Operator’s jacket run behind the steel.

What it means for the real buy

Many billboards have catwalks, lights or poles in front of them, and they almost always cover the bottom edge. Before each billboard is printed, we should ask the vendor for a photo of the actual location and keep the headline, logo and careers address out of the bottom fifth of the design. We should also build a poster-size version of each city's billboard, because some of the best locations near job sites and downtown streets are poster billboards rather than highway bulletins.

The next step is to repeat this render on a real 14-by-48 billboard on I-35, which is the size the plan actually budgets for. A phone photo of any I-35 bulletin would be enough to show the full-width design without changes.
